summary: Solid, multi-source, family-friendly core exists. The commonly told Yucatecan legend: two women of one village, Xkeban (looked down on by neighbours but kind to the poor, the sick and animals) and Utz-Colel (admired as proper and pure, but proud and cold). When Xkeban died, a sweet scent and fragrant flowers (xtabentun) came from her grave; when Utz-Colel died there was a bad smell and a thorny, scentless cactus (tzacam) grew. Envious, Utz-Colel returned as the Xtabay: a beautiful woman in white with long black hair who waits at night under a ceiba and combs her hair with cactus spines, calling to people on lonely paths so they get lost in the forest. Lesson: real goodness is in kindness, not in reputation or appearance; also a parental warning not to wander alone at night. Tell the story with the seduction, sexual, and death-by-devouring elements removed (see cautions); that leaves a clean 7-10 sentence beginner story.
facts: Setting: a village in Yucatan (Yucatec Maya region). Two women live there who are both beautiful but very different. [Wikipedia 'Xtabay'; Yucatan Today; mayan.org; Por Esto; Lifeder; Posta; Culturagenial]

Xkeban: the village looked down on her because of her reputation (many lovers / 'free' ways), but she was kind and generous. She helped the poor, cared for the sick, and cared for stray or injured animals. [Wikipedia; Yucatan Today; mayan.org; Por Esto; Lifeder; Culturagenial; Posta]

Utz-Colel: the village admired her as proper, virtuous and pure, but in truth she was cold, proud and unkind, especially to the poor and to animals. [Wikipedia; Yucatan Today; mayan.org; Por Esto; Lifeder; Posta]

When Xkeban died, a sweet scent of flowers rose from her; poor/humble people who knew her kindness buried her; fragrant flowers grew from her grave. The flower is the xtabentun. [Yucatan Today; Wikipedia; mayan.org; Por Esto; Lifeder; Posta; Culturagenial]

Xtabentun: a fragrant white-flowered wild vine (a morning glory, Turbina corymbosa, also listed as Ipomoea/Rivea corymbosa) that climbs over fences and hedges and along roads in Yucatan; it has no thorns. The Yucatecan honey-and-anise liqueur is named after it. [Wikipedia 'Xtabay'; Lifeder; mayan.org; Cuicuilco 2012 via search; es.wikipedia xtabentun (bebida)]

When Utz-Colel died, her body gave off a bad smell instead of the sweet scent she had expected, and a thorny cactus called tzacam grew at her grave (no perfume). [Yucatan Today; Wikipedia; mayan.org; Por Esto; Lifeder; Posta; Mexico Unexplained. Culturagenial says only 'barren grave']
Tzacam is thorny and scentless: it stands for bitterness / lack of kindness, the opposite of xtabentun, which stands for sweetness and compassion. [Por Esto; Lifeder; es.wikipedia Xtabay]

Jealous of Xkeban (or envious and proud), the spirit of Utz-Colel asked dark spirits / the gods to let her come back to the living. She returned as the Xtabay. [Wikipedia; Yucatan Today; mayan.org; Por Esto; Culturagenial; Mexico Unexplained]

The Xtabay appears at night, on lonely paths and near ceiba trees, as a very beautiful woman with long loose black hair and a white (often embroidered) dress; some versions add a sweet smell like xtabentun. [Wikipedia; Yucatan Today; Por Esto; Culturagenial; Posta; mayan.org]

She waits at or behind the ceiba and combs her hair with tzacam cactus spines. [Wikipedia; Yucatan Today ('brushing her hair'); mayan.org; Posta ('se peina' under the ceiba). The tzacam-spine comb detail is in Wikipedia, Yucatan Today does not name it; Por Esto/Lifeder omit it]
Her lure is aimed at people (traditionally men) walking alone at night; those who follow her are led into the forest/bush and get lost. [Wikipedia; Por Esto; Culturagenial; Yucatan Today; mayan.org]

The ceiba (Maya: ya'axche') is a sacred tree in Maya tradition: the 'world tree' that links the underworld, the earth and the sky. The name is glossed 'green tree' or 'first tree'. Ceibas were often left standing and planted in plazas. [Wikipedia 'Xtabay'; mayan.org; Por Esto ceiba article (2026); Bolles dictionary gloss via search]

What the legend teaches (consistent across sources): outward respectability does not make a person good, and a bad reputation does not make a person bad; kindness and a good heart are what count; pride, envy and coldness turn people sour. [Wikipedia; mayan.org; Por Esto; Lifeder; Culturagenial; Yucatan Today (implied)]

Everyday use: parents and grandparents tell the legend to warn children (and adults) not to wander alone at night or stay out drinking. [Wikipedia; Yucatan Today ('cautionary tale'); Mexico Unexplained]
Pronunciation: Xtabay is said roughly 'shta-BAI' (Yucatec x = 'sh'; Yucatan Today: shh-ta-BYE). Xkeban is roughly 'shke-BAN'. [Yucatan Today; Maya orthography convention]

Culture note: the story is a Yucatecan folk legend often described as mestizo (Maya and Spanish elements blended), not a pre-Columbian religious text. Well-known retellings: Jesus Azcorra Alejos, Diez Leyendas Mayas (1998); Roldan Peniche Barrera, El libro de los fantasmas mayas (1992); Antonio Mediz Bolio and Ermilo Abreu Gomez also retold it. [Wikipedia; es.wikipedia Xtabay; Yucatan Today; Culturagenial]
variants: Sisters or not: some tellings make Xkeban and Utz-Colel sisters, others just two women of the same village. Safe choice: 'two women in the same village'.
Which woman becomes the Xtabay: the great majority of sources say Utz-Colel (the proud 'pure' one). A few popular sites blur this or call Xkeban the Xtabay; treat Utz-Colel as the consistent core.

Utz-Colel's grave: most sources say a thorny scentless cactus (tzacam) grew there; Culturagenial says the grave simply stayed barren; Por Esto does not mention tzacam at all. Core = bad smell plus tzacam.

Spelling of names: Xtabay / X'tabay / X-tabay / Ixtabay / Xtabai; Utz-Colel / Utz Colel / Utz-colel / Utzkolel; tzacam / tsakam; xtabentun / xtabentún / x-táabentun (the last is the more exact Maya spelling per a 2012 Cuicuilco article). For a story in Spanish use Xtabay, Xkeban, Utz-Colel, xtabentún, tzacam, ceiba (ya'axche').

How the Xtabay ends her victims differs widely: lost in the forest; wake up sick and weak; thrown off cliffs or into wells; turned into a snake and eaten; found dead at the base of the ceiba covered in thorns. The only consistent part is that they are lured and lost. A Quintana Roo variant says she punishes drunks, thieves and criminals.
Other, separate origin stories of the Xtabay exist (Princess Suluay; punished couple of Zayil/Zaci) and a link to the old goddess Ixtab (rope / hanging). These are not part of the two-women core.

Physical description varies (white huipil and long black hair is the common one; some post-conquest versions give her bird feet, a trunk-like back or a demonic face). Use only the beautiful-woman-in-white image.
Some versions have a dark ending where she acts on seduction; this is the part to leave out for children.

maya_terms.meaning: the legendary woman of the forest paths who appears at night under the ceiba. The initial X (from Ix) is the Yucatec Maya feminine marker. Pronounced about 'shta-BAI'. Etymology of the name itself is uncertain/contested (do not state a meaning in the story).

name of the kind woman whom the village looked down on; the one whose grave bloomed with xtabentun. (A gloss of 'sinner' is only a reading of the story; not verified in a dictionary - do not translate in the story.)

name of the proud, proper-seeming woman who becomes the Xtabay. Commonly glossed utz = good and colel = lady/woman (general Yucatec knowledge; NOT confirmed by the sources consulted - use as a name only).

a fragrant white-flowered climbing vine (morning glory, Turbina corymbosa) that grows on fences and roads in Yucatan; in the legend, the flower from Xkeban's grave; also the name of a honey-anise liqueur. Widely repeated name gloss: 'vines that grow on stone' (not confirmed by a primary linguistic source).

a thorny, scentless cactus; in the legend, what grew from Utz-Colel's grave and what the Xtabay uses as a comb. Botanical identity varies by source (Mammillaria species, 'pol tsakam' = Mammillaria gaumeri); just say 'a thorny cactus'.
the ceiba tree, sacred world tree of the Maya (connects underworld, earth and sky); name glossed 'green tree' or 'first tree'. The Xtabay waits beneath or behind it.
the traditional embroidered dress worn by Maya women; the Xtabay's white dress is often described as a white embroidered huipil.

sources: https://www.proquest.com/docview/1461758952 (Romans 2013, Pacifica Graduate Institute thesis on La Xtabay; abstract only)
cautions: SEXUAL CONTENT: nearly every source describes Xkeban's scorned status as promiscuity / many lovers (some say 'prostitute') and the Xtabay as a seductress who lures men and in some versions kills or eats them after intercourse. Leave all of this out. Say only that the village looked down on Xkeban because of her reputation / 'what people said about her', or simply that people judged her unfairly. Do not use the words prostitute, lovers, seduce, sin.

DEATH/VIOLENCE: the legend involves two deaths and victims who are lost, sickened, thrown off cliffs or killed. Keep the deaths gentle (a woman 'passed away', 'when she died') and keep the Xtabay's effect to 'people who follow her get lost in the forest'. No snakes eating men, no torn-out hearts, no bodies found in thorns.
ALCOHOL: some versions and the xtabentun liqueur link the legend to drunk men. Do not mention drinking; if mentioning the xtabentun drink, only as 'a sweet honey drink' or omit it (safer: omit).
SUICIDE: the possible name link to the old goddess Ixtab (hanging / suicide) is scholarly and contested. Do not include it in a children's story.

HALLUCINOGENIC SEEDS: xtabentun seeds are described as psychoactive in the academic literature and Maya villagers are reserved about the plant's ritual use. Omit; present xtabentun only as a sweet-smelling white wild flower.

RELIGION AND BELIEF: the ceiba is genuinely sacred to the Maya; describe it respectfully ('the sacred ceiba tree'). Present the Xtabay as a story people tell ('dice la leyenda', 'cuentan que'), not as a claim that she is real or has been seen; some tourism sites report 'recent sightings' or a missing-person case that are anecdotal and not verified - do not repeat them.

CONTESTED ORIGIN: one Yucatan teacher (Edgar Perez Aguilar, quoted by Yucatan Today) argues colonial priests reshaped the legend and made the ceiba a dark symbol; scholars disagree on whether it predates colonisation. Call it only a 'Yucatecan legend' or 'cuento tradicional de Yucatan' and do not assert a pre-Hispanic origin.

MAYA NAME MEANINGS: do not give word-for-word meanings for Xtabay, Xkeban or Utz-Colel; the sources do not agree and I could not verify them in a dictionary (utz = good / colel = lady is general knowledge only). Etymology 'hidden vine' (one Spanish article) conflicts with Perez's lexicon link to Xtab / 'rope'; treat all as uncertain.

TZACAM IDENTITY: sources disagree on the exact cactus species. Say 'a thorny cactus called tzacam'. Whether the tzacam is described as a 'flower' differs (Lifeder 'cactus flower' vs others 'cactus'); prefer 'a thorny cactus'.
WHO IS THE XTABAY: keep Utz-Colel as the one who becomes the Xtabay (majority of sources). Do not mix in the Princess Suluay or Ixtab variants.
GENDER OF VICTIMS: traditional versions target men; one source says she can take any form or sex. For a children's story use neutral 'people who walk alone at night' or 'someone lost on the path'.

SOURCE QUALITY: no single authoritative academic or government text was fully readable (the Italian Sapienza PDF was an unreadable scan; the Cuicuilco and Redalyc PDFs were unreadable via fetch; the Romans thesis only as an abstract). The facts above are the overlap of Wikipedia (citing Romans 2013, Starr 1904, Azcorra Alejos 1998, Peniche Barrera 1992), Yucatan Today, Por Esto, Posta, Lifeder and others. Recommend a native Yucatec speaker or local teacher review the Maya terms before publishing.
